consensus_summary: Across all four blind responses, 'voice' symbolizes divine communication: God's or Christ's authoritative self-revelation, speech, command, and guidance addressed to humanity (Sinai, Psalm 29, the still small voice, the voice from heaven, and especially the Shepherd's voice in John 10 that His sheep hear and follow). Secondary senses (prophetic herald, inward Spirit guidance, theophanic power, testimony/accusation) are treated as contextual variants of the same core idea of a speaker's communicated message.
book_summary: The book defines voice as 'the words of the one who speaks,' and specifies that 'the Shepherd's voice is His words' — i.e., voice is a metonym for the spoken message/words of the speaker, exemplified by Christ's words to His sheep (John 10:27).
consensus_core_identification: Voice = the authoritative communicated speech of the speaker, paradigmatically God's/Christ's revelation and guidance which hearers are to recognize and obey (the Shepherd's voice heard by His sheep).
book_core_identification: Voice = the words of the one speaking; in the paradigm case, the Shepherd's (Christ's) voice is His words.
boundary_disagreement: None material. The book's phrasing 'the one who speaks' is formally general enough to cover any speaker, but the consensus also acknowledges human-voice cases (herald, bride/bridegroom, Abel's blood) as secondary senses, and Response C explicitly notes voice functions metonymically for the speaker and message. Both readings center on the Shepherd's voice as Christ's communicated words.
material_contradiction: None. The book's identification of voice with the speaker's words is precisely the communicative-content reading the consensus places at its core; the book merely omits the consensus's added emphases on authority, presence, and power without denying them.
rationale: Reduced to minimum cores, both say the same thing: voice stands for the words/message of the speaker, with Christ's voice to His sheep as the paradigm. The consensus dresses this in richer theological language (revelation, authority, obedience), but the book's terse metonymic definition ('the Shepherd's voice is His words') is the same referent in the same sense, not a boundary change or replacement. No cases admitted by the consensus are excluded by the book or vice versa; differences are wording and level of elaboration.
strongest_objection: One could argue the book REFINES by stripping the consensus's core down from 'divine self-revelation, presence, and authority' to a bare linguistic identification (voice = words), potentially excluding the theophanic-power and presence dimensions (Psalm 29, Sinai) that the consensus treats as central; and John 10:27 alone shows sheep hearing and following the voice without explicitly equating voice with 'words,' so the printed citation only partially establishes the definition.
